done.why: I lost every treasure twice, once when the balloon crashed and again when the Wizard took them. I left the mat and letter opener in a library I can't get back to, and I need them for the locked door. My lamp was dimming, and the glass-walled maze kept saying 'flickering dimly' whichever way I went. I had no idea what would get me further, so I stopped.

about: You're a treasure-hunter in the caverns south of a ravine. A senile, petulant Wizard lives there, along with the Empire's lost valuables. He keeps popping in to cast spells starting with F, and he steals whatever you pick up. The job is to work out the old machinery and monsters: a riddle door, a dragon you can goad, a hot-air balloon, a bank whose walls you can walk through, and a room that spins. The point is getting the treasures back to wherever he hoards them.

moments.note: The Wizard's look tells me what this place wants: pearls behind a stone door that asks a question, everything else past a room that won't keep still. That gave me a goal right away.
The yellow sphere was an illusion from 'Fantasize!', and the room 'has the grace to look embarrassed'.
The carousel room describes its own trick, and the hint about the stone door's grinding points me the right way.
'a well' got a hollow laugh. Only 'well' worked.
I goaded the dragon into following me to the ice. It melted the glacier on its own reflection and drowned. A great payoff.
I wasted a match because the receptacle was closed. The 'With a matchbook??!?' reply was funny, though.
I waited one turn too many, floated out of the volcano and died on the mountains. All my treasures went to the Wizard.
After respawning, walking south said 'You are on your own feet again', as if I were still in the basket.
Rummaging in the chest woke the princess, and she walked off on her own.
The Wizard whispered an F-word and my statuette and portrait vanished. I'd only just found them.
I found the locked door with the key inside. The mat and letter opener I'd need were stranded in the library when the balloon was lost.
I found the clay brick, and the black string from earlier suddenly made sense as a fuse.
The maze window's 'count' explanation was intriguing, but whichever way I went it only ever said 'flickering dimly' or went dark.

wished: I wished I could get my stuff back from the library after the balloon was gone. I'd dropped the mat and letter opener there just to make room.
I wished a short answer like 'a well' counted for the riddle.
I wished the carousel's 'works' gave me some lead. I never found a way to stop it, so every crossing was a coin toss.
I wished the maze window ever got brighter, so I could tell I was making progress.
I wished I knew where the princess and the unicorn went. I followed up and they had both vanished.

lines.line: It is all south of the ravine, his look says, every treasure the Empire mislaid, and much good may it do you; the pearls nearest, behind a stone door that asks a question, and the rest further in, past a room that will not keep still.
lines.why: This gave me my goal and a rough map in one sentence.

lines.line: the Wizard's word put it in the room, and the room, having no say in the matter, let it, and has the grace to look embarrassed about it now.
lines.why: A funny, charming way to tell me the sphere was an illusion.

lines.line: It will wait for her. You need not.
lines.why: A kind way of saying this isn't my puzzle yet.

lines.line: A thing that is turned can presumably be stopped, by somebody who finds the works.
lines.why: It planted a goal I never managed to follow up.

lines.line: There is a muffled explosion and the dragon, a puzzled expression on his face, dies.
lines.why: The best moment in the game for me.

lines.line: He keeps them; that is something. It is nowhere you have been yet.
lines.why: Some comfort after dying, and it pointed me onward.

fun.why: The dragon, the balloon and the bank were all fun to work out. The fun drained once the Wizard kept stealing things and the carousel made every trip a gamble.

engagement.why: The Wizard's hint gave me a purpose straight away, and I kept pushing for about 200 turns. Near the end, backtracking through the random carousel wore me down.

difficulty.why: The single puzzles were fair. Losing everything when I died, the Wizard's thefts, and leaving tools somewhere I couldn't return to made it pile up. The maze window gave me nothing to work with.

interestingness.why: A dense world. Things I picked up early, like the string and the newspaper, paid off later. The Wizard's random interruptions gave it a lively, hostile feel.

prose.why: Dry, witty and well paced. The extra lines on the sphere, the unicorn, the carousel and the doorway alarm were good to read and useful too.
